opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the simplicity was deliberate. There's a lot of excitement right now about using foundation models, the big open-vocabulary detectors and vision-language models, to label data automatically. But a lot of the claims are anecdotal: someone runs a model over a dataset, the boxes look pretty good, and the conclusion is that we don't need human annotators anymore. We wanted to ask a much more basic question in a controlled way. If you take off-the-shelf models, auto-label a dataset, and train a standard downstream detector on those labels, how does it compare to the same detector trained on human labels?

To answer that cleanly, you have to strip away as many confounding variables as possible. So we used well-known benchmark datasets, standard detector architectures, and fairly vanilla training recipes. We weren't trying to build the best possible auto-labeling pipeline with clever prompt engineering, ensembling, and heavy post-processing. If we'd done that, any result would be tangled up with all those choices, and it would be hard for anyone to tell what actually drove the outcome.

There's also a practical motivation. Most practitioners, the people at companies with real data problems, aren't going to build an elaborate research pipeline. They'll take a model off the shelf, pick a confidence threshold, and go. So we wanted the setup to reflect what someone would realistically do, so the findings would transfer to the real world.

And frankly, a simple setup is reproducible. Others can rerun it, poke at it, and extend it. I'd rather put out something clean that people can build on than something flashy nobody can verify. The interesting findings, like how much the confidence threshold matters and where auto-labels hold up versus fall short compared to human annotation, came through precisely because the setup didn't hide them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I get asked about a lot, and honestly the simplicity was the point. When we sat down to write that report, the question we wanted to answer wasn't "what's the fanciest way to auto-label data," it was "does this actually work at all, and under what conditions does it stop working?" And the moment you start layering in a lot of machinery, you lose the ability to answer that question cleanly.

So we picked a standard object detection setup, a well-understood dataset, a baseline detector that people know and trust, and then we varied one thing at a time. How much human-labeled data do you start with? How good does the model have to be before its predictions are worth using as labels? What happens when you feed those pseudo-labels back in? If I had thrown in a bunch of custom architectures or exotic training tricks, every result would come with an asterisk, and a reader couldn't tell whether the effect was from the auto-labeling or from something else we did.

The other piece is that I wanted practitioners to be able to read it and go, "okay, I could do this on Monday." A lot of the people who care about this problem aren't research labs, they're teams with a camera, a limited labeling budget, and a deadline. If the experiment only makes sense with a huge compute budget and six engineers, it doesn't really help them. A simple setup makes the takeaway portable.

And I'll be candid, simple setups are also where you discover the uncomfortable stuff. We found some failure modes, cases where the auto-labels confidently reinforced the model's own mistakes, and those were much easier to see and diagnose because there wasn't a lot of noise in the pipeline. I think that's the part of the report people underestimate. The goal wasn't to show the best number, it was to be honest about where the method breaks.

astra-6.text: We wanted to isolate the auto-labeling question. If we made the setup too complicated, it would be hard to tell whether a difference came from the labels or from some other choice in the pipeline. A simple setup gives us a clearer way to ask: how useful are these automatically generated labels for training an object detector? It’s a starting point for understanding that tradeoff, rather than trying to capture every real-world scenario in one experiment.

sol-6.1.text: We wanted to isolate the value of auto-labeling. If you make the experimental setup too complicated, it becomes hard to tell whether an improvement came from the labels, the model, or some other choice in the pipeline. Keeping it simple lets us ask a very practical question: how much manual labeling can you avoid, and what happens to the detector’s performance as you do that?
